title: The Next Twenty Years of the JVM
description: Two long-time Java voices look back at what changed the platform most since 2006 and make five concrete, falsifiable predictions for the next twenty years. Expect a live scorecard you can hold them to in 2046.
speaker: Lukas Brenner
speaker_bio: Lukas has taught Java to more than 9,000 developers and writes the weekly "Duke's Digest" newsletter. He keeps bees on the roof of his Vienna flat and names every hive after a JEP.

title: The Next Twenty Years of the JVM
description: Two long-time Java voices look back at what changed the platform most since 2006 and make five concrete, falsifiable predictions for the next twenty years. Expect a live scorecard you can hold them to in 2046.
speaker: Nora Halvorsen
speaker_bio: Nora wrote "Concurrency for Humans" and consults on JVM modernisation. She explains every concurrency concept with coffee orders and has never used a debugger in front of a client.

title: Virtual Threads in Production: What Nobody Told Us
description: Kestrel Payments moved a gateway handling 4,000 payments per second to virtual threads. This talk covers pinning on synchronized blocks, the ThreadLocal cache that blew up memory, and the dashboard that finally showed what was happening.
speaker: Ines Varga
speaker_bio: Ines moved Kestrel's payment gateway to virtual threads in 2025. Outside work she restores 1970s pinball machines and refuses to own a smartphone with more than 64 GB of storage.

title: Feature Stores Without the Hype
description: Do you need a feature store, or just a well-designed Postgres schema? Chiara compares both approaches using real scooter-demand forecasting at Parallax Mobility.
speaker: Chiara Bellini
speaker_bio: Chiara builds the data pipelines behind Parallax's e-scooter fleet in 14 cities. She makes her own pasta and claims it improves her SQL.

title: Designing Accessible Data Tables
description: Tables are where accessibility goes to die. Learn the markup, keyboard patterns and screen-reader announcements that make dense data usable for everyone, with before-and-after demos.
speaker: Sofia Lindqvist
speaker_bio: Sofia leads accessibility at Brightloom and screen-reads every UI she ships. She is a volunteer ice-hockey referee on weekends.

title: Inside the Garbage Collector: ZGC Live Tuning
description: A live session tuning ZGC on a train-scheduling workload, using JFR and GC logs to explain every decision. Bring your hardest GC questions.
speaker: Tomasz Wierzbicki
speaker_bio: Tomasz tunes the JVMs that schedule 3,000 trains a day across Central Europe. He once cut a GC pause from 800 ms to 2 ms and celebrated with a cake shaped like a heap dump.

title: RAG Is a Search Problem
description: Most retrieval-augmented generation failures happen before the LLM is ever called. Kwame shows how classic search techniques — BM25, query rewriting and re-ranking — fixed Mossgrove's assistant.
speaker: Kwame Mensah
speaker_bio: Kwame builds retrieval systems at Mossgrove and argues that most RAG problems are really search problems. He maintains a spreadsheet ranking every jollof rice he has ever eaten.

title: Event Storming for Skeptics
description: You think it is just sticky notes on a wall. Margot shows how a single four-hour session reshaped Quillstone's claims platform and saved a planned rewrite.
speaker: Margot Lefèvre
speaker_bio: Margot manages the claims platform team at Quillstone and is the company's unofficial Event Storming champion. She owns 412 colours of sticky notes.

title: Modelling Domains with Records, Sealed Types and Pattern Matching
description: Railway signalling rules are unforgiving. Greta shows how modern Java features make illegal states unrepresentable, and how the compiler became the team's best reviewer.
speaker: Greta Hoffmann
speaker_bio: Greta models railway signalling rules in modern Java at Ferrovia. She is learning the cello and practises in the server room because "the acoustics are great".

title: Running Kubernetes on a Shoestring
description: Cobalt Orchard runs production on second-hand servers and a very small budget. Viktor shares the setup, the failures and the monthly bill.
speaker: Viktor Sandberg
speaker_bio: Viktor runs Cobalt Orchard's Kubernetes clusters on hardware bought second-hand from a bankrupt bank. He heats his sauna with the waste heat from a homelab.

title: CSS Has Grown Up: Container Queries and :has()
description: Modern CSS replaced most of the JavaScript layout hacks we wrote in the 2010s. A fast-paced tour of container queries, :has(), cascade layers and subgrid in real client projects.
speaker: Mateo Fernández
speaker_bio: Mateo sits between design and code at Driftwood, a twelve-person studio in Valencia. He has not written a media query since 2024 and is very smug about it.

title: From COBOL to Java 25: A Five-Year Migration Diary
description: Five years, 2.3 million lines of COBOL and one insurance company that cannot stop for a day. Bram shares what worked, what failed and why they never did a big-bang rewrite.
speaker: Bram De Smet
speaker_bio: Bram is five years into moving Quillstone's COBOL policy engine to Java. He still keeps a printed copy of a 1987 COBOL manual on his desk "for emergencies".

title: Evaluating LLM Features Like You Test Code
description: If you would not ship code without tests, why ship prompts without evals? Amara shows Mossgrove's evaluation pipeline: golden datasets, LLM-as-judge and regression gates in CI.
speaker: Amara Okafor
speaker_bio: Amara runs the platform behind 200+ production models at Mossgrove. She is a competitive Scrabble player and holds a regional record for the word QUIXOTRY.

title: Threat Modelling Your Pull Requests
description: Threat modelling does not have to be a two-day workshop. Elif shows a ten-minute checklist that Kestrel's engineers apply to every PR touching sensitive data.
speaker: Elif Demir
speaker_bio: Elif runs Kestrel's internal red team and reviews every pull request that touches card data. She has found bugs in three password managers she will not name.

title: GraalVM Native Image: The Good, the Bad and the Reflection
description: Native images start in milliseconds — until reflection, resources and third-party libraries get in the way. Lukas walks through a real migration and the tools that make it bearable.
speaker: Lukas Brenner
speaker_bio: Lukas has taught Java to more than 9,000 developers and writes the weekly "Duke's Digest" newsletter. He keeps bees on the roof of his Vienna flat and names every hive after a JEP.

title: Observability That On-Call Engineers Actually Want
description: Dashboards nobody reads, alerts everybody ignores. Jonas shows how Cobalt Orchard cut pages by 70% by designing observability around the person who gets woken up.
speaker: Jonas Pietersen
speaker_bio: Jonas has been on call for Cobalt Orchard's smart-farming fleet for six years. He wrote an open-source pager that only wakes you up if the outage is actually your fault.

title: Game Loops for Web Developers
description: What can a web app learn from a game engine? Hana explains fixed time steps, interpolation and frame budgets, then applies them to a laggy React dashboard.
speaker: Hana Kobayashi
speaker_bio: Hana writes the physics engine behind Saltmarsh's space sim "Orbital Drift". Before games she spent four years building flight simulators for a satellite operator.

title: Hands-on: Build Your First Micronaut Service
description: Bring a laptop with Java 25. In two and a half hours you will build, test and containerise a Micronaut REST service backed by Postgres. Limited to 60 seats.
speaker: Oluwaseun Adeyemi
speaker_bio: Seun has run hands-on Micronaut workshops at 30+ meetups. He live-codes with a mechanical keyboard so loud that venues now ask him to bring a quieter one.

title: Hands-on: Prompt Engineering for Backend Developers
description: A practical workshop on structured outputs, tool calling and prompt testing, built around a mock clinical-guidelines assistant. No ML background needed. Limited to 60 seats.
speaker: Dev Raghunathan
speaker_bio: Dev leads AI engineering at Ondine Health, where agents help clinicians search 30 years of patient-care guidelines. He has run a marathon on every continent except Antarctica.

title: Software That Ships Freight: Lessons from 40 Million Parcels
description: Every software decision at Halcyon Freight ends up as a truck on a road. Rafael shares the architecture lessons that only show up at the scale of 40 million parcels a year.
speaker: Rafael Monteiro
speaker_bio: Rafael designed the routing platform that moves 40 million parcels a year for Halcyon Freight. He sails a 1962 wooden sloop called "NullPointer".

title: Structured Concurrency Explained with Coffee Orders
description: Structured concurrency, scoped values and cancellation, explained entirely through a busy café. You will never think about forking a subtask the same way again.
speaker: Nora Halvorsen
speaker_bio: Nora wrote "Concurrency for Humans" and consults on JVM modernisation. She explains every concurrency concept with coffee orders and has never used a debugger in front of a client.

title: Vector Search in Postgres: How Far Can pgvector Go?
description: Before you add a dedicated vector database, see how far plain Postgres gets you. Benchmarks on 50 million embeddings, index trade-offs, and when Chiara finally gave up.
speaker: Chiara Bellini
speaker_bio: Chiara builds the data pipelines behind Parallax's e-scooter fleet in 14 cities. She makes her own pasta and claims it improves her SQL.

title: Micro-Frontends: A Retrospective
description: Brightloom split its frontend into 19 micro-frontends and later merged them back into three. Felix explains what each step cost and what he would do differently.
speaker: Felix Aumann
speaker_bio: Felix co-founded Brightloom, which makes learning software for 4,000 schools. He split their frontend into 19 micro-frontends in 2022 and merged them back into three in 2025.

title: Project Valhalla: Value Classes for Everyday Developers
description: Value classes are coming. Tomasz shows what they change for memory layout and performance in ordinary business code — not just in benchmarks.
speaker: Tomasz Wierzbicki
speaker_bio: Tomasz tunes the JVMs that schedule 3,000 trains a day across Central Europe. He once cut a GC pause from 800 ms to 2 ms and celebrated with a cake shaped like a heap dump.

title: Outbox, Inbox and Sagas: Reliable Messaging at Scale
description: How Halcyon Freight processes 1.2 billion events a day without losing a parcel. Transactional outbox, idempotent consumers and sagas with real failure stories.
speaker: Priya Castellanos
speaker_bio: Priya owns Halcyon's messaging backbone, which handles 1.2 billion events a day. She speaks five languages and is learning Finnish "for fun".

title: Secrets Management Without Tears
description: API keys in environment variables, tokens in Slack, passwords in the wiki. Elif shows a pragmatic path from secret sprawl to short-lived credentials.
speaker: Elif Demir
speaker_bio: Elif runs Kestrel's internal red team and reviews every pull request that touches card data. She has found bugs in three password managers she will not name.

speaker: Rafael Monteiro

title: Mobile Web Performance on a Budget Phone
description: Your users do not have your laptop. Leilani profiles a real web app on a 2019 budget handset and fixes it live, one long task at a time.
speaker: Leilani Kahale
speaker_bio: Leilani makes the Parallax rider app fast on cheap phones. She tests every release on a 2019 budget handset she calls "The Potato".

speaker: Yasmin Haddad
speaker_bio: Yasmin builds the clinician-facing tools at Ondine Health and ran the hospital network's first chaos day. She is a trained pastry chef.

title: Tooling Is UX: Building Internal Tools People Love
description: Internal tools are usually built last and loved least. Zofia shares how Saltmarsh's editor team runs user research with game designers and ships weekly.
speaker: Zofia Nowak
speaker_bio: Zofia builds the internal editors that Saltmarsh's designers use every day. Her rule: if a tool needs a manual, the tool is wrong.

description: Replace mocks and shared test databases with real dependencies in throwaway containers. Bring a laptop with Docker installed. Limited to 60 seats.
